caseStudies.cardHeading: Every enquiry answered in under a minute
caseStudies.title: One inbox, one calendar, zero missed enquiries
caseStudies.summary: New patient enquiries arrived across three websites, two inboxes and a phone line. We connected them into a single pipeline that acknowledges, qualifies and books — before reception has opened the door.
caseStudies.challenge: Riverside had grown from one practice to three in eighteen months, and each site had inherited its own way of handling new patients. Enquiries landed in a shared inbox, a website form that emailed a personal address, and a phone line that went to voicemail after 5pm. Nobody could say how many enquiries came in last month, and the practice manager was spending most of Monday reconstructing what had happened over the weekend.

approach.title: One front door
approach.body: Every route in — three website forms, two inboxes and the out-of-hours voicemail — now writes to a single intake record. Voicemail is transcribed automatically so a phone enquiry looks exactly like a web one.

approach.title: An acknowledgement that sounds like them
approach.body: A reply goes out within a minute in the practice's own tone, confirming what was asked and attaching the right next step. Drafts are generated against a tight brief and a library of the manager's own past replies.

approach.title: Booking without the back-and-forth
approach.body: The reply carries a link to live availability filtered by treatment type and clinician. The slot lands in the practice management system and the patient's calendar at the same time.

approach.title: A Monday that starts with a number
approach.body: A Friday digest reports volume by site, source and treatment, and flags any enquiry that has gone quiet for more than 48 hours.

caseStudies.outcome: Within the first month the practice moved from a median first response of just under seven hours to 48 seconds, and tripled the share of enquiries that turned into a booked appointment. Reception recovered roughly a day a week.

quote.text: We didn't buy anything new. Joyce just made the things we already paid for talk to each other, and suddenly Monday morning wasn't a fire drill.
quote.name: Priya Nandra

caseStudies.cardHeading: Quotes that used to take a day, out in nine minutes
caseStudies.title: A quote builder that reads the drawings
caseStudies.summary: Every quote meant one director reading a PDF drawing pack by hand and rebuilding a spreadsheet from scratch. We built the tool that reads the pack, prices it against their real rates, and hands back an editable draft.
caseStudies.challenge: Halloway lost work to slower, worse joiners simply because they quoted later. Pricing a job meant the managing director sitting down with a PDF drawing pack, counting units by hand, and rebuilding last month's spreadsheet with this month's timber prices. It took the best part of a day, it only happened in the evenings, and the estimate quality depended entirely on how tired he was.

approach.title: Read the pack, not the summary
approach.body: Drawing packs are parsed page by page, pulling schedules, dimensions and finish specifications into a structured item list with a confidence score and a link back to the source page for anything uncertain.

approach.title: Their rates, not generic ones
approach.body: Fifteen years of completed jobs became the pricing model: material rates, wastage assumptions, and the labour hours the workshop actually books rather than the ones the old spreadsheet assumed.

approach.title: A draft, never a decision
approach.body: The output is an editable quote with every line traceable to a drawing reference. Nothing is sent without a human pressing send — the tool removes the typing, not the judgement.

approach.title: Learning from the edits
approach.body: Every correction is logged. Lines that get edited repeatedly surface in a monthly review so the underlying rates get better rather than staying wrong.

caseStudies.outcome: Quotes now go out the same morning the pack lands, averaging nine minutes of director time instead of most of a day. Halloway more than doubled the number of quotes issued per week without adding an estimator.

quote.text: I stopped losing jobs to people who weren't better than us, just faster. That's the whole thing, really.
quote.name: Tom Halloway

caseStudies.cardHeading: Client onboarding, from three weeks to three days
caseStudies.title: Onboarding that runs itself while you sleep
caseStudies.summary: Fourteen documents, four systems and a compliance checklist held in one person's head. We turned onboarding into a tracked sequence that chases itself and leaves an audit trail nobody has to assemble.
caseStudies.challenge: Onboarding a new client at Northgate took roughly three weeks, most of it waiting. Fact-finds were emailed as attachments and came back incomplete. ID verification lived in a separate portal nobody remembered to check. The compliance file was assembled at the end, from memory, by whoever had the time — which made annual review season genuinely stressful.

approach.title: One sequence, not fourteen emails
approach.body: A single tracked onboarding record drives everything. The client sees one link that always shows what is done, what is outstanding, and what happens next.

approach.title: Chasing without nagging
approach.body: Reminders escalate on a schedule the firm set, and stop the instant a document arrives. Advisers are pulled in only when something genuinely needs a human.

approach.title: The compliance file builds as you go
approach.body: Identity checks, source-of-funds evidence and suitability notes file themselves against the right client record with timestamps, so the audit trail exists before anyone asks for it.

approach.title: Nothing new to learn
approach.body: Advisers kept working in the CRM they already used. The sequence writes into it rather than replacing it.

caseStudies.outcome: Onboarding now completes in a median of three days, every file is audit-complete at the point of completion, and no adviser has written a chase email since launch.

quote.text: Annual review season used to be three weeks of archaeology. Now the file is just already right.
quote.name: Deborah Ashworth

caseStudies.cardHeading: One stock figure, true across every channel
caseStudies.title: Selling in four places without overselling in any
caseStudies.summary: A shop floor, a website, a marketplace and a pop-up stall, all quietly disagreeing about how many of something existed. We made one number true everywhere and gave the owner a Monday report she trusts.

metrics.label: To close the books each week

caseStudies.challenge: Sable & Fern sold the same stock through a physical shop, a Shopify store, a marketplace listing and seasonal pop-ups. Each channel kept its own count, and reconciliation was a Sunday-evening spreadsheet job. Overselling a one-off ceramic piece meant an apologetic refund email and a customer who did not come back.

approach.title: A single source of truth
approach.body: Stock levels live in one place. Every channel reads from and writes back to it within seconds of a sale, so the shop floor and the website can never drift apart.

approach.title: Rules for the awkward cases
approach.body: One-off and low-stock items reserve on add-to-basket and release on timeout. Pop-up sales are captured offline and reconciled the moment the stall reconnects.

approach.title: Purchase orders that suggest themselves
approach.body: Reorder points are calculated from actual sell-through per line rather than a flat threshold, and draft purchase orders arrive already filled in.

approach.title: A Monday report worth reading
approach.body: One page: what sold, what is running out, what has not moved in ninety days, and what it is costing to hold.

caseStudies.outcome: Overselling has effectively stopped, six hours of weekly reconciliation disappeared, and the weekly close now takes twelve minutes instead of an evening.

quote.text: I used to dread Sunday nights. Now the number is just right, and I can spend that time buying things people actually want.
quote.name: Marianne Okoye

caseStudies.cardHeading: A team that actually uses the tools it was given
caseStudies.title: From 'I'm not sure about all this AI' to daily use
caseStudies.summary: Brightpath had bought licences nobody was using. We ran the training that turned scepticism into a set of concrete, safe, everyday habits — and wrote the policy that let people relax.
caseStudies.challenge: Brightpath had rolled out AI licences across its office and management staff and seen almost no uptake. The reasons were reasonable: nobody knew what was safe to type into it given the sensitivity of care records, nobody had seen it do anything relevant to their actual job, and a general anxiety that it was there to replace them.

approach.title: Start with the fear, not the features
approach.body: The first session addressed what the tools do and do not do, what happens to what you type, and where the line sits for care data. Confidence came from clarity, not enthusiasm.

approach.title: Their work, not generic examples
approach.body: Every exercise used real Brightpath tasks: rota conflict letters, CQC evidence summaries, family update emails, supervision note drafting.

approach.title: A policy people could actually follow
approach.body: A one-page responsible use policy — three green lanes, three red lines, and who to ask — written to be read once and remembered.

approach.title: Champions, then a check-in
approach.body: Six champions were trained more deeply and given a running channel. A structured check-in at sixty days caught the teams that had quietly stopped.

caseStudies.outcome: Ninety days after training, 78% of trained staff were using the tools weekly against a baseline near zero, and registered managers reported recovering around five hours a week from documentation.

quote.text: The difference was that Joyce trained us on our job, not on the software. Nobody left that room thinking it was going to replace them.
quote.name: Ade Fashola
